core.text: 2 Related Work

A large body of work improves LLM reasoning by increasing test-time computation via sampling, search, and aggregation. Chain-of-Thought prompting elicits intermediate rationales that improve multi-step accuracy (Wei et al., 2022), while self-consistency aggregates multiple sampled rationales/answers to reduce variance (Wang et al., 2022). Beyond pure sampling, several lines explicitly branch over intermediate states, including algorithmic tree search for language-model agents and reasoning-time search controllers (Chen et al., 2024; Teng et al., 2025). Program-guided variants offload parts of reasoning to execution, reducing arithmetic and symbolic errors through tool-based computation (Gao et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2022). These methods establish that more test-time compute helps, but do not by themselves specify how to allocate verification cost across intermediate branching.

Verifier-centric pipelines train or use models that score correctness of solutions or intermediate steps. Early work trained verifiers for math word problems and showed that reranking/selection with a verifier can substantially boost accuracy (Cobbe et al., 2021). Process supervision and step-level reward models provide dense feedback over reasoning traces and can guide selection among candidates (Lightman et al., 2023). Separately, LLM-as-a-judge has emerged as a practical evaluation and selection primitive for open-ended generations (Zheng et al., 2023). Our work is aligned with verifier-based selection, but focuses on where to spend verifier calls: we treat learned scoring as pre-verification prioritization and rely on explicit verification for acceptance.

Rather than spending a fixed budget everywhere, recent work studies how to allocate test-time compute to maximize accuracy per unit cost. Compute-optimal allocation demonstrates strong gains from problem-dependent budgeting and analyzes several allocation primitives, including lookahead-style intermediate exploration (Snell et al., 2024).

A complementary direction is to reduce wasted computation by enforcing structure during generation. Constrained decoding and grammar-based generation restrict outputs to syntactically valid forms, improving reliability in structured tasks (Hokamp and Liu, 2017; Post and Vilar, 2018). Tool-use frameworks also emphasize structured interfaces (actions with arguments) to make downstream execution and validation well-defined (Schick et al., 2023). Similarly, we enforce a structured move interface and use cheap, deterministic feasibility checks to eliminate clearly invalid candidates before invoking an expensive verifier.

Retrieval-augmented generation improves factuality and reasoning by conditioning generation on retrieved context (Lewis et al., 2020; Borgeaud et al., 2022). Large-scale retrieval inside language modeling (e.g., RETRO-style approaches) further demonstrates that retrieval can substitute for some parametric memory and improve generation quality (Borgeaud et al., 2022). In contrast, our retrieval component (when enabled) targets operator/move reuse rather than external knowledge retrieval; it is most closely related to reusing verified sub-steps within a structured search space.

Our setting is also conceptually adjacent to contextual bandits and sequential resource allocation: at each state, the system must choose which candidates to evaluate under a limited budget, using context-dependent uncertainty to decide where evaluation has high marginal value(Li et al., 2010). However, we do not cast training or inference as a bandit algorithm, since we have supervised verifier labels from exploration logs and our primary objective is improved verification-call efficiency under a fixed generator–verifier interface. We therefore treat bandit-style allocation as related conceptual framing rather than a direct baseline in our experiments.
3 Problem Formulation: verification-cost-limited reasoning

We study intermediate-step reasoning under a verification-call cost model. Given an input problem xx, a reasoning system repeatedly proposes candidate next-step updates and may invoke a verifier to check step validity. We treat verifier invocations as the dominant marginal cost, and aim to minimize verifier calls subject to high task accuracy.

We represent a reasoning state as w=(r,s,ℓ),w=(r,s,\ell), where ss is the current symbolic trace (e.g., equations or partial derivation), ℓ\ell is an explicit constraint context (e.g., known bindings, domain constraints, tracked invariants), and rr is the remaining verification budget. We omit an explicit time component; time is subsumed into rr as a budgeted resource.
At state ww, the system forms a candidate set of moves
ℳ⁡(w)=ℳgen​(w)∪ℳret​(w),\mathcal{M}(w)\;=\;\mathcal{M}_{\text{gen}}(w)\ \cup\ \mathcal{M}_{\text{ret}}(w), (1)

where ℳgen​(w)=Gen​(w)\mathcal{M}_{\text{gen}}(w)=\mathrm{Gen}(w) are newly proposed moves and ℳret​(w)\mathcal{M}_{\text{ret}}(w) are retrieved moves (e.g., cached operators) whose preconditions match the current context. Each move is a structured hypothesis m=(op,args)m=(\texttt{op},\texttt{args}) that can be deterministically parsed into an operator with well-defined arguments. A move induces an updated state via a deterministic application operator w′=Apply⁡(w,m).w^{\prime}=\mathrm{Apply}(w,m).
This structured interface is essential: it provides a domain where deterministic feasibility checks are meaningful, without attempting to soundly analyze arbitrary free-form text.

A verifier 𝒱⁡(w,m)∈{0,1}\mathcal{V}(w,m)\in\{0,1\} returns whether applying mm is an acceptable reasoning step at ww. The verifier may be an LLM judge, tool execution, or any other expensive oracle; our cost metric counts verifier invocations. We emphasize that gating and verification play different roles: gates cheaply rule out moves that violate explicit deterministic constraints, while the verifier adjudicates semantic correctness among remaining candidates.
Let Solve⁡(x)\mathrm{Solve}(x) denote producing a final answer for problem xx. We seek policies that optimize the accuracy–cost frontier:

maxπ𝔼⁡[𝟏​{Solve⁡(x)​is correct}]s.t.𝔼⁡[#​verifier calls]≤B.\begin{split}\max_{\pi}\ &\mathbb{E}\big[\mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{Solve}(x)\ \text{is correct}\}\big]\\ \text{s.t.}&\quad\mathbb{E}\big[\#\text{verifier calls}\big]\leq B.\end{split} (2)
We focus on policies that allocate verification at intermediate states, where branching is large and uniform verification is expensive.
4 Method

Our core hypothesis is that state-level verification allocation yields better accuracy--cost tradeoffs than uniform verification, because local uncertainty varies widely across states within a single problem11 1 Note, we do not perform multi-step rollout evaluation to optimize a learned reward; our policy is single-step at each visited state and allocates verifier calls, not rollout depth. This distinction matters empirically because lookahead-style PRM search can underperform budget-matched best-of-NN in prior work; our method targets a different bottleneck: which intermediate candidates receive expensive verification.. We implement this as a three-stage gated competition pipeline:
Deterministic feasibility gates reject moves that violate explicit necessary conditions under the structured interface (no verifier calls).
Competitive scoring ranks surviving moves using a hybrid heuristic that decomposes structural progress and a learned pre-verification residual.
State-conditional allocation chooses k⁡(w)k(w) moves to verify, spending more verification budget when the local decision is uncertain.
4.1 Deterministic feasibility gates
We apply two deterministic feasibility predicates and retain only moves that pass both:

ℳ†​(w)={m∈ℳ(w):𝒢struct(w,m)=1∧𝒢ctx(w,m)=1}\begin{split}\mathcal{M}^{\dagger}(w)\;=\;&\{m\in\mathcal{M}(w):\\ &\mathcal{G}_{\text{struct}}(w,m)=1\ \wedge\ \mathcal{G}_{\text{ctx}}(w,m)=1\}\end{split} (3)

Gate 1: structural compatibility. 𝒢struct​(w,m)\mathcal{G}_{\text{struct}}(w,m) rejects moves that fail deterministic checks such as parseability of (op,args)(\texttt{op},\texttt{args}), symbol scope, and operator applicability to the current symbolic form in ss. These checks operate only on the structured move representation and the explicit context ℓ\ell.

Gate 2: constraint compatibility. 𝒢ctx​(w,m)\mathcal{G}_{\text{ctx}}(w,m) rejects moves that contradict the current constraint context ℓ\ell. Let Ctx⁡(w)\mathrm{Ctx}(w) denote extracted constraints from ww and let Δ⁡(w,m)\Delta(w,m) denote constraints newly introduced by applying mm. We define:

𝒢ctx(w,m)=𝟏[Consistent⁡(Ctx⁡(w)∪Δ⁡(w,m))∧¬Violates(Ctx(w),Δ(w,m))].\begin{split}\mathcal{G}_{\text{ctx}}(w,m)=\mathbf{1}\Big[&\mathrm{Consistent}\big(\mathrm{Ctx}(w)\cup\Delta(w,m)\big)\ \wedge\ \\ &\neg\mathrm{Violates}\big(\mathrm{Ctx}(w),\Delta(w,m)\big)\Big].\end{split} (4)

The gate does not guarantee global semantic soundness. Instead, the gates are deterministic necessary-condition checks with respect to the structured interface and the explicitly tracked constraints in ℓ\ell. Passing the gates does not imply correctness; failing the gates indicates an explicit violation (e.g., undefined symbol, inapplicable operator type, direct contradiction with tracked invariants).
4.2 Competitive scoring: structure + learned pre-verification residual
Among gated survivors, we rank moves using
h⁡(w,m)=Dtype​(w′,w⋆)+rθ​(w,m),w′=Apply⁡(w,m),\begin{split}h(w,m)\;&=\;D_{\text{type}}(w^{\prime},w^{\star})\;+\;r_{\theta}(w,m),\\ w^{\prime}&=\mathrm{Apply}(w,m),\end{split} (5)
where DtypeD_{\text{type}} is a structural distance between states and rθr_{\theta} is a learned residual trained for top-kk selection under a verifier-call budget.

We instantiate DtypeD_{\text{type}} as a latent structural distance computed from an LLM encoder. Let e⁡(⋅)e(\cdot) denote the frozen (or lightly tuned) embedding function given by the generator backbone, applied to a canonical serialization of a state. We compute embeddings for the post-move state and the goal specification:
zw′=e((w′),zw⋆=e(w⋆).z_{w^{\prime}}=e((w^{\prime}),\qquad z_{w^{\star}}=e(w^{\star}).
We then define
Dtype​(w′,w⋆)=d⁡(zw′,zw⋆),D_{\text{type}}(w^{\prime},w^{\star})=d(z_{w^{\prime}},z_{w^{\star}}), (6)

where d⁡(⋅,⋅)d(\cdot,\cdot) is a distance metric in embedding space. While cosine distance is a simple choice, we find that a learned distance function performs better in our settings. Crucially, DtypeD_{\text{type}} is not used as a hard reachability gate; it serves only as a soft structural prior in Eq. (5), since approximate goal tests can be brittle.

predicts which feasible moves are worth spending verifier calls on under a finite budget. It does not accept or reject moves; acceptance is determined only by the verifier 𝒱⁡(w,m)\mathcal{V}(w,m). Thus rθr_{\theta} affects efficiency (and indirectly success under a fixed budget) by prioritizing verification, but cannot by itself introduce invalid steps.
4.2.1 Training data from verifier-labeled candidate lists

We train rθr_{\theta} from exploration runs on training problems using the same generate–gate–verify loop as at test time. Each run visits a sequence of states; at each visited state ww we log: (i) the post-gating candidate set ℳ†​(w)\mathcal{M}^{\dagger}(w), and (ii) verifier labels for all candidates in that set:
y⁡(w,m)=𝒱⁡(w,m)∈{0,1},m∈ℳ†​(w).y(w,m)\;=\;\mathcal{V}(w,m)\in\{0,1\},\qquad m\in\mathcal{M}^{\dagger}(w). (7)

This yields a dataset of state-wise candidate lists with sparse positives, where positives are exactly the moves the verifier would accept under the same structured interface. Optionally, when the system commits an accepted move, we also record the transition (w,m,w′)(w,m,w^{\prime}) along the accepted trace for auxiliary analysis (e.g., downstream utility among multiple acceptable moves).
4.2.2 Embedding model for rθr_{\theta}

We also parameterize rθr_{\theta} as a lightweight scorer over LLM latent embeddings of the state and the move. Let e⁡(⋅)e(\cdot) denote the same LLM embedding function used above, applied to serialized inputs. We compute
zw=e⁡(w),zm=e⁡(m),z_{w}=e(w),\qquad z_{m}=e(m),
We then score with a small MLP head:
rθ​(w,m)=gθ​([zw;zm;zw⋆]).r_{\theta}(w,m)=g_{\theta}\!\big([z_{w};z_{m};z_{w^{\star}}]\big). (8)

Including zw⋆z_{w^{\star}} allows the residual to model instance-specific preferences relative to the goal, while DtypeD_{\text{type}} provides a direct embedding-distance progress signal. In our instantiation, e⁡(⋅)e(\cdot) is frozen and only gθg_{\theta} is trained.
4.2.3 Loss: within-state ranking from verifier feedback
Because rθr_{\theta} is used for top-kk selection, we train it as a ranking model within each state. For each state ww, define:

ℳ+​(w)={m∈ℳ†​(w):y⁡(w,m)=1}ℳ−​(w)={m∈ℳ†​(w):y⁡(w,m)=0}.\begin{split}&\mathcal{M}^{+}(w)=\{m\in\mathcal{M}^{\dagger}(w):y(w,m)=1\}\\ &\mathcal{M}^{-}(w)=\{m\in\mathcal{M}^{\dagger}(w):y(w,m)=0\}.\end{split} (9)
We sample pairs (m+,m−)(m^{+},m^{-}) with m+∈ℳ+​(w)m^{+}\in\mathcal{M}^{+}(w) and m−∈ℳ−​(w)m^{-}\in\mathcal{M}^{-}(w) and minimize the logistic pairwise ranking loss

ℒrank​(θ)=𝔼w​𝔼m+∼ℳ+​(w),m−∼ℳ−​(w)[log⁡(1+exp⁡(rθ​(w,m+)−rθ​(w,m−)))].\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\text{rank}}(\theta)=&\mathbb{E}_{w}\;\mathbb{E}_{m^{+}\sim\mathcal{M}^{+}(w),\,m^{-}\sim\mathcal{M}^{-}(w)}\\ &\Big[\log\big(1+\exp(r_{\theta}(w,m^{+})-r_{\theta}(w,m^{-}))\big)\Big].\end{split} (10)
Minimizing (10) encourages verifier-acceptable moves to rank ahead of rejected moves. (Equivalently, one can swap the sign convention; we adopt the convention that lower h⁡(w,m)h(w,m) ranks higher.)

Verifier labels provide strong local supervision (which candidates are acceptable at a given state), but they may not distinguish among multiple acceptable moves by downstream utility. When we have accepted trajectories τ=(w0,m0,w1,…,wL)\tau=(w_{0},m_{0},w_{1},\dots,w_{L}) that reach a correct solution, we add a weak cost-to-go signal based on remaining steps. Let

be the remaining number of accepted moves to termination along τ\tau. We use g⁡(⋅)g(\cdot) as an extra supervision target that prefers moves that advance toward termination in fewer verified steps. Concretely, we regress the residual toward this signal:
ℒtraj​(θ)=𝔼(wi,mi)∈τ​[(rθ​(wi,mi)−α​g​(wi))2],\mathcal{L}_{\text{traj}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(w_{i},m_{i})\in\tau}\Big[\big(r_{\theta}(w_{i},m_{i})-\alpha\,g(w_{i})\big)^{2}\Big], (11)
where α\alpha rescales the step-count target to match the residual magnitude. Our final objective is
ℒ⁡(θ)=ℒrank​(θ)+λ​ℒtraj​(θ),\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathcal{L}_{\text{rank}}(\theta)+\lambda\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{traj}}(\theta), (12)
where ℒrank\mathcal{L}_{\text{rank}} is the primary signal and ℒtraj\mathcal{L}_{\text{traj}} is a weak signal.
4.3 State-conditional verification allocation

Let ℳ†​(w)\mathcal{M}^{\dagger}(w) denote the move set after gating. We compute scores {h⁡(w,m):m∈ℳ†​(w)}\{h(w,m):m\in\mathcal{M}^{\dagger}(w)\} and use their dispersion as a proxy for local decision uncertainty:
σ2​(w)=Var⁡({h⁡(w,m):m∈ℳ†​(w)}).\sigma^{2}(w)=\mathrm{Var}\Big(\{h(w,m):m\in\mathcal{M}^{\dagger}(w)\}\Big). (13)
We then allocate a state-conditional verification budget
k⁡(w)=clip⁡(kmin,kmax,kbase​(1+β⁡(σ⁡(w)/σ¯−1))),k(w)=\mathrm{clip}\Big(k_{\min},k_{\max},k_{\text{base}}\big(1+\beta(\sigma(w)/\bar{\sigma}-1)\big)\Big), (14)

and verify only the top-k⁡(w)k(w) moves by h⁡(w,m)h(w,m). When scores are concentrated, verifying many candidates is wasteful; when many candidates are close, additional verification yields higher marginal value.
4.4 Algorithm

At each state, multiple candidates compete via h⁡(w,m)h(w,m) under a limited verification capacity k⁡(w)k(w). Verifier outcomes provide high-precision feedback used to train rθr_{\theta} via within-state ranking and to update any optional retrieval/cache mechanism, aligning with an intuition of parallel proposal, competitive selection, and global feedback.
5 Experiments
5.1 Goal and empirical questions

We study verification-cost-limited reasoning, where the dominant marginal test-time cost is invoking an expensive verifier 𝒱⁡(w,m)\mathcal{V}(w,m) on intermediate moves. Prior work (Snell et al., 2024) demonstrates that test-time compute allocation at the problem level can yield significant efficiency gains over uniform best-of-N by conditioning on problem difficulty. Our scientific question is whether finer-grained, state-level allocation provides additional benefits by combining (i) deterministic feasibility structure at the move interface and (ii) uncertainty-aware state-level allocation of verification effort.
5.2 Setup

We evaluate on MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021) using the 500-problem test split from Lightman et al. (2023), consistent with Snell et al. (2024). Following their protocol, we define problem difficulty as a function of the base model’s capabilities: we estimate pass@1 from 64 samples per problem and bin questions into five quintiles of increasing difficulty. We use two-fold cross-validation on difficulty bins to avoid confounding bin selection with evaluation. For additional validation, we include results on GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) (1,319 test problems).

Unless stated otherwise, the backbone generator is Llama 3.2 1B. The verifier is a process reward model (PRM) trained via Monte Carlo rollouts following Wang et al. (2024), consistent with the verifier setup in Snell et al. (2024).

All methods share (i) the same structured move interface, (ii) the same generator Gen\mathrm{Gen} (and retrieval module, if enabled), and (iii) the same verifier 𝒱\mathcal{V}. Thus, differences are attributable to selection and allocation rather than model identity.
We treat each verifier invocation as one unit of dominant cost and report
Cver=∑t=1T|𝒬⁡(wt)|,C_{\text{ver}}\;=\;\sum_{t=1}^{T}\big|\mathcal{Q}(w_{t})\big|, (15)

where tt indexes visited verification decision points (including retries/backtracking) and 𝒬⁡(wt)⊆ℳ⁡(wt)\mathcal{Q}(w_{t})\subseteq\mathcal{M}(w_{t}) is the subset of moves queried to the verifier at wtw_{t}. For completeness, we also report total calls (generation + verification), but conclusions are unchanged in our call-dominated regime.
5.3 Baselines
All baselines use the same generator Gen\mathrm{Gen}, the same structured move interface, and the same verifier 𝒱\mathcal{V}.

Best-of-NN samples NN complete solutions and selects the answer with highest aggregated verifier score, following the “best-of-N weighted” selection from Snell et al. (2024) that marginalizes across solutions with the same final answer.

Beam Search maintains a beam of partial states and expands each state by proposing candidate moves. Following Snell et al. (2024), we keep the top-bb partial states after each expansion step using PRM scores, and query 𝒱\mathcal{V} according to the baseline’s acceptance rule. We report the total verifier calls accumulated across the entire search. We select b=4b=4. This represents intermediate-state verification with uniform allocation (fixed beam width throughout).

Majority Voting samples NN complete solution traces and returns the most frequent final answer among samples. No verifier is used for selection; this tests whether verification provides value beyond sampling diversity.
5.4 Main results: accuracy–cost frontier

Table 1 reports overall accuracy and verifier-call cost on MATH. Across all methods, our objective is not to maximize accuracy at any cost, but to improve the call-efficiency frontier, i.e., achieve higher end-task correctness under fewer expensive verifier invocations.

Our approach achieves 55.2% accuracy while using an average of 44.8 verifier calls. This outperforms all solution-level sampling baselines at the same nominal budget (6464 calls): Best-of-NN reaches 42.4%, Majority Vote reaches 44.6%, and Beam Search reaches 51.8%. Notably, we improve over the strongest listed baseline (Beam Search) by +3.4 points while using 30% fewer verifier calls (44.8 vs. 64). In this setting, the gains are consistent with the hypothesis that decision difficulty is heterogeneous within a single problem: allocating verification locally at ambiguous branching points is more effective than spending the same calls uniformly or only at the solution level.

Verifier calls are the primary cost metric. Our method improves accuracy over solution-level sampling baselines while using substantially fewer verifier calls.
5.5 Budget-matched comparison under fixed generation budgets

To test whether intermediate-state allocation provides benefits beyond solution-level selection, we compare several common inference-time strategies under matched verifier-call budgets. For a target budget CverC_{\text{ver}}, we run each method with the same number of generations per problem (so the x-axis is a shared generation budget) and count verifier calls as the dominant cost.

Figure 2 shows accuracy as a function of generation budget N∈{2,4,8,16,32,64,128}N\in\{2,4,8,16,32,64,128\}. Across budgets, our method is consistently more call-efficient, achieving the best accuracy among budget-matched strategies, especially at moderate-to-large budgets. Notably, beam search provides a strong improvement over solution-level selection at small-to-moderate budgets (consistent with the value of intermediate branching), but saturates earlier than our method. This pattern supports our thesis: how verification is distributed across intermediate states (via gating, hybrid scoring, and state-conditional k⁡(w)k(w)) can materially change the accuracy achievable under a fixed verifier-call regime.
5.6 Ablations: disentangling gating, scoring, and allocation

To isolate the effect of feasibility filtering, the “gates-only” condition verifies all surviving candidates after gating, without changing the verification policy otherwise. Subsequent ablations incrementally add scoring and adaptive allocation while keeping the same gated candidate set.

Configuration Verifier calls ↓\downarrow Acc (%) ↑\uparrow Verify-all (no gates) 64.0 45.0 Gates-only 58.0 47.6 Gates + DtypeD_{\text{type}} (fixed kk) 54.0 51.8 Full 44.8 55.2 Table 2: Ablations on MATH. “Gates-only” verifies all gated survivors to isolate pruning effects.

The result ins shown in table. 2. First, feasibility gating alone reduces verifier calls from 64 to 58 while improving accuracy (45.0→\rightarrow47.6), indicating that a substantial fraction of generated moves are deterministically invalid and waste verification budget. Second, adding structural distance scoring further improves accuracy (47.6→\rightarrow51.8) while reducing calls, showing that even among feasible candidates, informed prioritization matters. Finally, state-conditional allocation provides the largest marginal gain: adaptive k⁡(w)k(w) reduces verifier calls by an additional 17% (54.0→\rightarrow44.8) while increasing accuracy to 55.2%. This confirms that uncertainty varies meaningfully across intermediate states, and that reallocating verification effort locally yields a better accuracy–cost frontier than uniform allocation.
5.7 Backbone and dataset variations

We evaluate how backbone capacity affects the accuracy–budget curve of our state-level selective verification policy on MATH-500 (Figure 3). Using the same framework and budget sweep, upgrading the generator from Llama 3.2 1B to Llama 3.2 3B yields a consistent improvement at every budget. In particular, the 3B backbone achieves substantially higher accuracy under small budgets (e.g., 222^{2}–242^{4} generations), and continues to improve up to 272^{7} generations, where it reaches 67.0% on MATH-500.

A key qualitative observation is that the benefit of a stronger backbone is largely complementary to our allocation mechanism: both backbones exhibit a similar monotonic scaling trend with additional verifier budget, while the stronger backbone shifts the entire curve upward. Moreover, the high-budget regime with Llama 3.2 3B approaches the dashed Llama 3.1 70B reference line, suggesting that state-level selective verification can partially substitute for model scaling by converting additional test-time budget into accuracy gains, while still benefiting from improved proposal quality as the backbone strengthens.
6 Conclusion

We study test-time reasoning under a verification-cost-limited setting, where the dominant marginal expense comes from calling an external verifier on intermediate steps. Our approach combines deterministic feasibility gating, hybrid pre-verification scoring, and uncertainty-aware state-level allocation, and consistently outperforms best-of-NN, beam search, and majority voting under matched verifier-call budgets. Ablations confirm that each component contributes non-redundant gains: gating reduces wasted verification, scoring improves which candidates are worth checking, and adaptive allocation concentrates effort on ambiguous decision points. Overall, our findings suggest that finer-grained control over where verification is applied is a key lever for improving the efficiency of test-time reasoning.
6.1 Limitations

Selective verification cannot exceed the quality of the candidate generator.If no feasible correct move is proposed at a given decision point, no allocation or verification policy can recover the correct reasoning path. In practice, we observe this limitation most clearly on the hardest MATH instances (difficulty bin 5), where performance is bounded by the backbone model’s ability to propose correct intermediate steps. This mirrors the observation in Snell et al. (2024) that, beyond a certain difficulty regime, additional test-time compute yields diminishing returns unless proposal quality improves through larger models or better pretraining.

Feasibility gates also rely on what constraints are explicitly tracked in the context ℓ\ell and on the expressiveness of the structured move interface. Constraints that are not represented in ℓ\ell cannot be filtered deterministically and must be resolved by the verifier. As a result, our gates are intentionally high-precision but incomplete, and their effectiveness depends on the quality of the structured interface rather than on full semantic understanding.
